newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-New York City sandhogs star in working class novel.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-New York City sandhogs star in working class novel.

text.p: Tom Kelly thinks he may be the only onetime sandhog who ever earned a master's degree at Harvard.
Harvard of course is American shorthand for prestige. Sandhog is shorthand for a New York City tunnel-digger.
Odd as that combination seems, the 35-year-old Kelly separates himself further from the pack by being the only tunnel-digging Harvard graduate ever to publish a novel.

"Payback" tells the story of the Adare brothers and the working class labourers, the ultra-violent Irish and Italian mobsters and the powers who ruled the streets of New York City during the money-fevered 1980s. Deeper inside are revelations about Irish-American ethnicity in a changing world and about Bronx neighbourhoods where the sharp brogue grows fainter as "white flight" leaves only skeletons from a former life.

It is also about sandhogs, so much so that Kelly dedicates the book not only to his late father but to the 23 men who have died building New York City Water Tunnel No. 3, a job he held while in college. He says his reason for writing the book in the first place was to feature the guys underground and an entire class of people left out of recent U.S. literature.
NOBODY WRITES ABOUT WORKERS ANYMORE
"Nobody writes about working people, not in fiction, not in film, not in novels, not in short stories. We're in a society where less and less people work with their hands," he told Reuters recently.
Kelly found an outlet for his views on the labour movement, working for years as a Democratic Party organiser and also running a non-profit organisation for trade unions.

The failure of New York Mayor David Dinkins to win re-election in 1993 paid off for supporter Kelly, leaving him without a political job but lots of time. "I might not be sitting here today if he had won," Kelly said.

Some critics have called "Payback" a flip side to Tom Wolfe's "Bonfire of the Vanities," whose leading characters were struck with fear of being maimed by outer-borough New Yorkers from the kind of neighbourhood where Kelly's characters live and breathe, for better or for worse.

Kelly, while accepting the Bonfire comparison as a compliment, says the working class is where he also lives. "The life of the sandhog is just as fascinating to me as a doctor or a lawyer or whatever," he said.
WHEN BEING A SANDHOG DELIVERS
That life works on more than one level in the novel.

The story revolves around Billy and Paddy Adare. Billy works in the tunnels for money, a summer job that acts as a bridge to a life in law school. Billy, the "good" brother, works underground, legitimately busting rocks to forge a life away from the grime and danger that killed his father.

Paddy, older and rougher than Billy, works above ground but below the law, whacking people around, an Irish enforcer violently shaking down builders and unions. Paddy wants to shed his fat and return to the glory that almost made him an Olympic boxer but he is on the wrong side of the law and the life he leads cannot provide glory, just pain.

For Billy, the sandhog life is a passage to something different, something sought, even if his plan gets derailed by the violence and mayhem of Paddy's world. Billy, a loose regeneration of the author, harbours desires similar to Kelly's. Kelly says he sees his time in the tunnels as a vital link to what followed, that New York City Water Tunnel No. 3 was somewhow a deliverance.

"I turn and walk ... I slog through the muck and water, and think of how this tunnel provided me with a passage. It was my pipeline from blue-collar roots to the white-collar world. I am the only high school graduate in the history of my family. Digging this tunnel enabled me to become the first to earn a living without breaking my back," he said after a return visit to the underground.
"I worked as one of those guys and it makes up a realism you couldn't have had without the experience," he said. "Those facts from my times down there are very accurate."
Kelly, appropriately wedged in a neighbourhood Irish bar, rests with his thoughts. "I just hope the sandhogs get more recognition than they ever had," he said.
They probably hope he does too.
